value.overview: The White-crowned Sparrow (Zonotrichia leucophrys) is a medium-sized New World sparrow of North America. Adults are recognized by their boldly striped black-and-white crown, gray face and breast, brown back, and pink or yellowish bill. It is one of the most familiar migratory sparrows in Canada and the United States. In Costa Rica, it is an exceptionally rare visitor rather than a regular wintering species, with only scattered documented records.
value.classification: The species belongs to the sparrow family Passerellidae and the genus Zonotrichia. Several geographically distinct subspecies are recognized across its broad North American range.
value.identification: Adults have a crisp black-and-white striped crown, a gray face and underparts, brown wings and back, and a small pinkish or yellowish bill. The crown pattern is especially distinctive, although immature birds have a brown-and-tan striped crown and can resemble other Zonotrichia sparrows. White-crowned Sparrows often forage on the ground with a characteristic double-footed scratching motion. Their clear, whistled song is well known on the breeding grounds but is generally not expected from birds encountered in Costa Rica.
value.rangeHabitat: White-crowned Sparrows breed across much of Alaska and Canada and in western and northern parts of the United States, using tundra edges, open coniferous woodland, shrublands, mountain slopes, and other semi-open habitats. During migration and winter, they occupy brushy fields, weedy margins, scrub, gardens, and woodland edges. In Costa Rica, the species is an accidental or exceptionally rare visitor. Documented records include observations at Isla del Coco and Rancho Quemado in the Osa region, rather than a regularly distributed national population.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant across most of its range, it generally moves south in autumn and north in spring. Costa Rica lies well south of its normal wintering range, so occurrences there are rare, irregular, and likely reflect exceptional displacement or unusual movement rather than an established migration route.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs mainly in northern North America and in suitable mountain and northern habitats farther south. The female usually builds an open-cup nest low in shrubs, on the ground, or among low vegetation, using grasses, roots, moss, and other plant material. She typically lays several pale or bluish eggs marked with brown. The female performs most incubation, while both adults feed and tend the young. White-crowned Sparrows commonly defend territories with their distinctive whistled song.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists largely of seeds, grains, buds, berries, and other plant material, supplemented by insects and other small invertebrates, especially during the breeding season. White-crowned Sparrows usually feed on the ground, often beneath shrubs or at the edges of fields. They may scratch through leaf litter, pick seeds from bare soil, or visit ground feeders. Their feeding habits in Costa Rica are poorly documented because the species is so rarely recorded there.
value.behavior: White-crowned Sparrows are active, mostly terrestrial birds that frequently forage in loose flocks outside the breeding season. They run or hop across open ground, pause to scan for danger, and retreat quickly into dense cover when disturbed. Birds often roost in shrubs at night. Males sing from exposed perches during breeding, and the species shows strong regional variation in song. In Costa Rica, records are too few to describe consistent local behavior.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered broadly stable for conservation purposes, with regional declines reported in some areas. Costa Rica has no known resident population and receives only rare, irregular individuals.
